## Funiculars and colorful houses: what to see in Valparaíso and Viña del Mar, Chile

### Valparaíso

Valparaíso is the country's main port and one of the oldest cities in South America. Its name translates as "Paradise Valley." Valparaíso is the capital of the province of the same name, which also includes Easter Island and the Juan Fernández Archipelago. One of the city's calling cards is its fifteen funicular cars, built around a century ago to connect the flat port district with neighborhoods on the hills. Each lift has its own name and serves as a kind of landmark. From aboard, you can simply enjoy the magnificent view of the lower part of the city.

Valparaíso is a city of sailors and poets, the pearl of the Pacific, a paradise valley. Built across the hills, it makes extensive use of an unusual form of public transport: funiculars. The city has 15 lifts, some built more than 100 years ago. Visitors can enjoy beach time, admire the natural surroundings, and explore local sights.

A good place to start is the Hill of the Immaculate Conception, which offers a spectacular view of the city. Another feature is the charming houses with bright roofs and wrought-iron fences. In Valparaíso, travelers should also visit the Museum of Murals, stop by Pablo Neruda's house, see the exhibits at the Maritime Museum, and stroll through Sotomayor Square.

## Valparaíso: a city on the hills

### Valparaíso and Viña del Mar: a heavenly coastal pairing!

Viña del Mar is Chile's main beach resort, located 10 km from Valparaíso. Its mild climate, subtropical scenery, palms, banana trees, numerous parks, and sandy beaches make it a very inviting place to relax. The National Botanical Garden of Chile is located here, and interesting museums occupy old colonial mansions.

## Varadero: Cuba's fantastic beaches!

Varadero lies on the Hicacos Peninsula, 130 km north of Havana. It offers 20 km of soft sandy shoreline, warm Atlantic waters, and an endless row of hotels.

These are wonderful beaches with fine snow-white sand and remarkably azure water, along with diving centers. Varadero's beaches rank among the three best in the world. Visitors come to swim and sunbathe, listen to salsa rhythms, play golf, dance in discos, and sip rum. Ambrosio Cave, with its rock paintings, lies near Varadero. A dolphinarium is located on the grounds of a fairly large lake.

Venado Tuerto combines the business life of an agricultural region with the everyday pace of a city. Beyond professional meetings, visitors can explore the central San Martín Square, the municipal cultural center, and the Cayetano Silva Regional Museum.

The city appeals to delegations interested in more than production alone: workforce training, advisory services, and agribusiness management. We use Venado Tuerto as a base for technical visits to nearby sites and conversations with industry specialists. Meeting agendas are tailored to the group's goals; free time is left for exploring the city independently.

## Veracruz: Mexico's port city

Veracruz is a port city on the Gulf of Mexico. Ten to fifteen years ago, Veracruz had a reputation for being unattractive and dusty, until Governor Miguel Alemán launched an investment program to transform the city.

Today Veracruz is a romantic and distinctive city. The air smells of the salty sea, the streets are no longer dusty or dirty, many beautiful new buildings have appeared, and the historic center is on full display. Veracruz is famous for delicious coffee served at every turn. Don't miss the chance to enjoy a cup at the best-known historic Gran Cafe del Portal, near the port, on the grounds of an old monastery.

## Let's go to the Veracruz Carnival!

Every year since 1866, Veracruz has hosted a carnival, considered the second most important in Latin America after Rio de Janeiro's carnival. For 9 days before Ash Wednesday (usually in February), residents in bright costumes parade through the streets, sing, dance, and compete. Musical groups and dance schools arrive from across the country. Ticketed spectator stands are set up along the waterfront. At the end of the carnival, an effigy called Coque, symbolizing everything bad, is burned.
